title: USPS Unveils New Rangoli Diwali Stamp Ahead of Festival Ceremony
excerpt: The Forever stamp, featuring artist Sangita Bhutada's rangoli photographed by Bijay Dixit, will be unveiled Oct. 21 at the Embassy of India in Washington — a decade after the first U.S. Diwali stamp.
body:
• The U.S. Postal Service has unveiled a new Diwali stamp featuring a photograph of a rangoli, with the first-day-of-issue ceremony set for Wednesday, Oct. 21, at the Embassy of India in Washington, D.C.
  • The design shows artist Sangita Bhutada's intricate rangoli — blue, orange, green, red and white on a purple background — photographed by Bijay Dixit and designed by Jennifer Arnold; the stamp will be sold in panes of 20 as a Forever stamp.
  • How to get it: order through usps.com/shopstamps, call 844-737-7826, use USA Philatelic by mail, or buy at Post Office locations nationwide. Ceremony attendees must register in advance at usps.com/diwalistamp.
  • The new issue arrives a decade after the 2016 debut Diwali stamp, which followed a community campaign that began in 2004; Diwali's main day in 2026 falls on Nov. 8.

The U.S. Postal Service has unveiled a new Diwali stamp celebrating the festival of lights, announcing the issue on Sept. 17, 2026, with a first-day-of-issue ceremony scheduled for Wednesday, Oct. 21, at the Embassy of India in Washington, D.C.

Shibani Gambhir, the Postal Service's sales intelligence and support vice president, will serve as the dedicating official. Retail sales and cancellations run from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. ET, followed by the ceremonial unveiling and reception at 6 p.m. ET at 2107 Massachusetts Ave. NW. News of the stamp is being shared under the hashtag #DiwaliStamp.

Context & Background

The 2026 stamp features a photograph of a rangoli — a vibrant floor pattern traditionally made from colored rice powder, chalk and flower petals to bring good fortune during Diwali. Artist Sangita Bhutada, who has been creating rangolis for nearly 30 years, crafted the intricate design in blue, orange, green, red and white with starch-based colored powder and colored sand. The photograph, by Bijay Dixit, is set against a purple background. William J. Gicker served as the project's art director, and Jennifer Arnold designed the stamp.

The new issue arrives a decade after the Postal Service's first Diwali stamp. The Citizens' Stamp Advisory Committee announced that issue on Aug. 23, 2016, and the first-day-of-issue dedication took place on Oct. 5, 2016, at the Consulate General of India in New York, in the presence of Consul General Riva Ganguly Das, Rep. Carolyn Maloney, Diwali Stamp Project Chair Ranju Batra, USPS Vice President Pritha Mehra and Ambassador Hardeep Singh Puri.

That 2016 stamp was the culmination of a campaign that began in 2004, when Dr. Shailendra Kumar and Dr. Piyush Agrawal of the Association of Indians in America wrote to the advisory committee requesting a Diwali stamp. Community organizations kept up the pressure for years, pointing out that the Postal Service had already issued stamps for Christmas, Kwanzaa, Hanukkah and Eid.

The 2016 design featured a photograph of a traditional diya oil lamp by Sally Andersen-Bruce, with Greg Breeding as designer and Gicker — back again for the 2026 project — as art director.

Impact & Analysis

The 2026 stamp will be issued as a Forever stamp, sold in panes of 20. That designation matters: the stamp will always be equal in value to the current First-Class Mail 1-ounce price, no matter when it is bought.

A second design signals that Diwali now holds a settled place in the Postal Service's holiday lineup rather than standing as a one-off gesture. Stamp issues are chosen years in advance through the Citizens' Stamp Advisory Committee; a new design for the same festival indicates the committee sees continuing public demand and relevance.

For collectors, a new Diwali issue creates a matched pair with the 2016 stamp, now ten years old. For the broader public, it puts Hindu festival imagery onto everyday mail: rangoli, diyas and the five-day autumn festival's celebration of the triumph of good over evil.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, a Diwali stamp is one of the most visible forms of mainstream recognition the community can receive — postage that travels through every corner of the country carrying the imagery of their festival. The choice of the Embassy of India as the venue for the first-day ceremony gives the unveiling a formal, binational character, placing the festival within the cultural conversation between India and the United States.

The design itself centers diaspora craft: Bhutada's nearly three decades of rangoli-making and Dixit's photography, developed by an American design and art-direction team. It is, in miniature, the kind of cultural collaboration that defines the community's place in the U.S.

What's Next

The first-day-of-issue ceremony on Oct. 21 is the stamp's official launch. Attendees must register in advance at usps.com/diwalistamp. The stamps will be available through the Postal Store at usps.com/shopstamps, by calling 844-737-7826, by mail through USA Philatelic, or at Post Office locations nationwide.

The main day of Diwali in 2026 falls on Nov. 8, roughly two weeks after the stamp's debut — timing that gives the issue a natural window on festival-season mail.
